name: Voxels rasterized as geometry
text:
# Voxels rasterized as geometry
## Overview
Voxels rasterized as geometry is an [object-order volume rendering](#10725-object-order-volume-rendering.md) technique that treats volumetric data as a collection of 3D primitives (typically cubes or quads) and renders them using standard rasterization pipelines [G]. It solves the problem of visualizing scalar field data by converting it directly into mesh geometry, projecting it into screen space rather than sampling rays through the volume [G]. It differs from its siblings, such as [Splatting](23-splatting.md) (which projects soft blobs) or [Texture slicing](25-texture-slicing.md) (which samples 3D textures), by generating explicit geometric primitives for the volume elements, allowing for precise occlusion culling and standard [shading models](#837-shading-models.md) at the cost of high primitive counts [G].

## Shared principles
The family shares the fundamental mechanism of converting scalar field data into geometric primitives that are submitted to the graphics pipeline [G].

1. **Primitive Generation**: Each occupied voxel is represented by one or more geometric primitives. The most common representation is a cube (6 faces, 8 vertices for shared shading, or 24 vertices for flat shading) or a set of quads representing visible faces [G].
2. **Coordinate Transformation**: Voxel indices $(i, j, k)$ are transformed into [world space](#2511-voxel-coordinate-systems-and-conversion.md). For a dense grid with bounds $P_{min}$ and $P_{max}$ and dimension $N_{dim}$, the world position $P_{world}$ of a voxel center is calculated as:
$$
P_{world} = P_{min} + \frac{I_{voxel}}{N_{dim}} \times (P_{max} - P_{min})
$$
For unit voxels, this simplifies to $P_{world} = I_{voxel} \times V_{size}$, where $V_{size}$ is the voxel dimension [S4, unofficial].
3. **Rasterization**: The generated primitives are transformed into clip space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix and rasterized. Visibility is determined by the depth buffer (z-buffer) or a back-to-front painter's algorithm if transparency is required [G].
4. **Culling**: To manage performance, frustum culling is applied to exclude voxels outside the camera view. Back-face culling is often enabled to discard faces oriented away from the camera, calculated by the dot product of the view-space normal and the view vector [G].

## Subtopics

### [Binary Volume Rendering (Opacity Thresholding)](1015-binary-volume-rendering-opacity-thresholding.md)
[Binary volume rendering](#1015-binary-volume-rendering-opacity-thresholding.md) is a technique where voxels are classified as either completely opaque or completely transparent based on whether their scalar density exceeds a specific threshold. It reduces the rendering problem to projecting opaque geometric primitives onto the image plane, effectively visualizing the iso-surface corresponding to the threshold interface. Unlike [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) methods that integrate optical properties along rays, this approach treats the volume as a collection of discrete opaque objects, relying on standard rasterization visibility techniques such as the z-buffer or a back-to-front painter's algorithm. It is primarily used for isolating highly opaque structures, such as bone in medical imaging, where a clear surface boundary is desired.

### [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md)
[Naive Voxel Rendering](#1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md) is an object-order volume rendering technique that represents every occupied voxel in a dense grid as a full geometric cube (or visible faces thereof) and submits these primitives to the graphics pipeline for rasterization. It solves the problem of visualizing scalar field data by converting it directly into mesh geometry, differing from [image-order ray-casting](#3161-image-order-ray-casting.md) methods by projecting geometry into screen space rather than sampling rays through the volume. Unlike optimized variants such as [Sparse Voxel Rasterization](3032-sparse-voxel-rasterization.md) or [SVO LOD Management](2990-svo-lod-management.md), this method generates primitives for all voxels without Level of Detail (LOD) reduction or greedy meshing, resulting in massive vertex counts for large scenes.

### [Intensity-based Sparse Voxel Storage](1775-intensity-based-sparse-voxel-storage.md)
Represents volumetric data by sorting voxels by intensity and using a histogram to index contiguous runs, treating intensity as run-length encoding. It differs from [Binary Volume Rendering](1015-binary-volume-rendering-opacity-thresholding.md) by supporting multi-level intensity and from [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md) by eliminating per-voxel intensity storage. Choose this when rendering large volumes with many identical intensity values to reduce memory bandwidth.

### [OpenGL Display List Voxel Rendering](2220-opengl-display-list-voxel-rendering.md)
[OpenGL Display List Voxel Rendering](#2220-opengl-display-list-voxel-rendering.md) is a technique that pre-compiles voxel geometry into OpenGL 1.0 fixed-pipeline display lists to enable fast, repeated rendering without re-sending vertex data. It is distinguished from sibling methods like [Vertex Array Object Voxel Rendering](2226-vertex-array-object-voxel-rendering.md) and [Geometry Shader Processing](2524-geometry-shader-processing.md) by its reliance on legacy API commands and its trade-off of significantly higher memory usage for superior per-frame render times.

### [Vertex Array Object Voxel Rendering](2226-vertex-array-object-voxel-rendering.md)
Vertex Array Object (VAO) Voxel Rendering is a method that converts voxel data into explicit geometric primitives (quads) stored in GPU memory, leveraging OpenGL's VAO and VBO mechanisms for efficient rasterization. It differs from [Geometry Shader Processing](2524-geometry-shader-processing.md) by pre-computing and storing all vertex data in video memory rather than generating geometry procedurally per frame, and from [Instancing with Procedural/Shader Generation](2794-instancing-with-procedural-shader-generation.md) by using explicit vertex buffers instead of instanced attributes. This approach trades higher video memory usage for simplified rendering pipelines and negligible main memory overhead.

### [ClearView Vertex Shader](2468-clearview-vertex-shader.md)
The [ClearView Vertex Shader](#2468-clearview-vertex-shader.md) is a geometry reconstruction technique that generates voxel face geometry entirely within the vertex shader using `gl_VertexID`, eliminating the need for CPU-side vertex attribute buffers or geometry shaders. It reconstructs 54,000 faces per cell, each consisting of 4 vertices and 2 triangles, by fetching pre-packed face, vertex, and edge data from GPU textures. It is distinguished from sibling methods like [Instancing with Procedural/Shader Generation](2794-instancing-with-procedural-shader-generation.md) by its explicit reliance on texture-based attribute lookups for LOD and line-drawing logic, and from [Geometry Shader Processing](2524-geometry-shader-processing.md) by performing primitive assembly in the vertex stage rather than the geometry stage.

### [Geometry Shader Processing](2524-geometry-shader-processing.md)
This family of techniques utilizes the GPU [Geometry Shader](#4369-geometry-shader-quads.md) (GS) to generate geometric primitives (cubes, quads, lines, or strips) directly from point or triangle inputs, enabling the rasterization of volumetric data without pre-computed mesh buffers. It solves the problem of dynamic geometry generation for voxel-based rendering by offloading primitive assembly to the GPU, allowing for real-time updates and adaptive detail. It differs from [Voxels rasterized as geometry](27-voxels-rasterized-as-geometry.md) by explicitly leveraging the GS stage for primitive expansion rather than relying solely on vertex buffers or fixed-function instancing.

### [Voxel Billboard Rendering](2554-voxel-billboard-rendering.md)
[Voxel Billboard Rendering](#2554-voxel-billboard-rendering.md) is a volume visualization technique that represents a 3D scalar field (such as a cloud volume) as a set of 2D quads (billboards) positioned at specific voxel locations within the volume grid. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering volumetric data by converting it into geometry that can be processed by standard rasterization pipelines using instanced rendering. Unlike [Binary Volume Rendering (Opacity Thresholding)](1015-binary-volume-rendering-opacity-thresholding.md) which discards data below a threshold, or [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md) which may render every voxel as a cube, this method explicitly generates billboard instances with per-instance position and scale attributes, relying on CPU-side sorting and generation rather than compute shaders or single large buffer storage.

### [Instancing with Procedural/Shader Generation](2794-instancing-with-procedural-shader-generation.md)
[Instancing with Procedural/Shader Generation](#2794-instancing-with-procedural-shader-generation.md) renders a voxel model by submitting a single draw call that instances a base geometric primitive (typically a unit cube) for each occupied voxel. It solves the [CPU](#10688-naive-sdf-generation-cpu.md) bottleneck of issuing individual draw calls for thousands of voxels by packing per-voxel data (position, color) into a single buffer and using the graphics pipeline's instancing mechanism to transform and color them procedurally. It differs from [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md) by reducing API overhead to a single call, and from [Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering](5849-voxel-fragment-shader-rendering.md) by computing the voxel's spatial position in the vertex/geometry stage rather than reconstructing it purely from fragment shader texture lookups.

### [SVO LOD Management](2990-svo-lod-management.md)
Not given in the sources.

### [Sparse Voxel Rasterization](3032-sparse-voxel-rasterization.md)
A real-time high-fidelity radiance field rendering system that integrates an efficient rasterizer with a multi-level sparse voxel scene representation. It adaptively fits sparse voxels into different levels-of-detail. Choose this for high-quality rendering of complex scenes with varying density.

### [Base Renderer Geometry](3902-base-renderer-geometry.md)
[Base Renderer Geometry](#3902-base-renderer-geometry.md) is a method for rendering voxel data by converting occupied voxel indices into explicit geometric primitives (cubes, squares, or lines) and submitting them to the graphics pipeline for rasterization. It solves the problem of visualizing scalar field data by treating voxels as discrete 3D objects rather than volume textures. It differs from [Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering](5849-voxel-fragment-shader-rendering.md) by generating geometry in CPU-side or vertex-shader-side buffers rather than computing ray-marching in the fragment shader, and from [Splatting and Point-based Rendering](4975-splatting-and-point-based-rendering.md) by using explicit polygonal faces instead of billboards.

### [Quad-to-Geometry Assembly](4604-quad-to-geometry-assembly.md)
[Quad-to-Geometry Assembly](#4604-quad-to-geometry-assembly.md) converts a list of axis-aligned quads (typically generated by greedy meshing or voxel culling) into a flat, GPU-ready vertex buffer and index buffer. It solves the problem of translating abstract quad primitives into the specific memory layouts required by WebGL/OpenGL `BufferGeometry` or `Mesh` objects. It differs from sibling methods like [Instancing with Procedural/Shader Generation](2794-instancing-with-procedural-shader-generation.md) by pre-computing all vertex data on the CPU, whereas instancing pushes the geometry generation into the vertex shader.

### [Debug and Visualization](4974-debug-and-visualization.md)
This family renders auxiliary geometry and cross-sectional views to inspect the spatial extent, selection state, and internal structure of voxel data during rendering. It solves the problem of spatial orientation and debugging by overlaying wireframes or slices onto the framebuffer, distinct from [Binary Volume Rendering (Opacity Thresholding)](1015-binary-volume-rendering-opacity-thresholding.md) which visualizes the volume content itself rather than its container or structure.

### [Splatting and Point-based Rendering](4975-splatting-and-point-based-rendering.md)
Not given in the sources.

### [Hexagonal Prism Voxel Rendering](5626-hexagonal-prism-voxel-rendering.md)
[Hexagonal Prism Voxel Rendering](#5626-hexagonal-prism-voxel-rendering.md) is a [geometry-based volume rendering](#4395-specific-material-and-geometry-rendering.md) technique that represents occupied voxels as hexagonal prisms rather than cubes to reduce aliasing artifacts and provide smoother surface appearances. It differs from cubic voxel methods by utilizing a specific hexagonal vertex layout and instanced rendering to optimize draw calls, addressing the jagged edges inherent in axis-aligned cubic representations.

### [Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering](5849-voxel-fragment-shader-rendering.md)
[Voxel Fragment Shader Rendering](#5849-voxel-fragment-shader-rendering.md) is a fragment-shader-based technique that renders voxels as solid cubes by performing ray-AABB (Axis-Aligned Bounding Box) intersection in screen space. It computes surface normals, samples colors, and applies fog within the fragment shader, effectively moving the geometric intersection logic from the CPU or vertex stage into the per-fragment pipeline. This method differs from [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md) by handling visibility and shading entirely in the fragment shader via [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md), and from [Sparse Voxel Rasterization](3032-sparse-voxel-rasterization.md) by treating each voxel as a discrete geometric primitive with explicit intersection math rather than relying on sparse data structures for culling.

### [Voxelization via Rasterization](6352-voxelization-via-rasterization.md)
This family generates a [voxel representation](#10852-voxel-based-representation.md) of 3D geometry by projecting input primitives onto 2D planes, rasterizing them for coverage, and mapping the results to 3D voxel coordinates. It distinguishes itself from siblings like [Binary Volume Rendering](1015-binary-volume-rendering-opacity-thresholding.md) and [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md) by leveraging established 2D rasterization pipelines instead of brute-force 3D traversal or simple thresholding.

#### Geometry Loading (Non-Triangle)
Loads basic geometry parameters (size, type) for non-triangle volumes (cylindrical/spherical) [S3, unofficial]. It copies geometry size and type to device symbols and sets a flag indicating the geometry is not triangles [S3, unofficial].

#### TLAS Instance Traversal
Manages transformed voxel objects by storing local [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) structures and applying inverse rotations during ray queries [S4, unofficial]. It transforms rays into instance local space via inverse rotation (transpose, since the matrix is orthogonal) [S4, unofficial]. The `VoxelInstance` contains a local `BrickPool` (BLAS), rotation matrix, and bounding sphere [S4, unofficial].

#### Rasterizing Proxy Geometry
Not given in the sources.

#### Point-Based Chunk Rendering
Each chunk is rendered as a collection of points using `GL_POINTS`, with vertex attributes for position, normal, and texture coordinates [G]. It binds the chunk VAO, sets model/view/projection matrices, and calls `glDrawArrays(GL_POINTS, 0, num_vertices)` [G]. A pitfall is that meshes are always updated on the GPU even if empty to prevent floating quads when destroying blocks near chunk borders [G].

### [3D Cube Projection and Rasterization](6678-3d-cube-projection-and-rasterization.md)
A method to render a 3D cube by transforming its 8 vertices into 2D screen coordinates using perspective projection and drawing the visible faces (front, top, bottom) as polygons.

### [Sparse Voxel Storage and Management](8435-sparse-voxel-storage-and-management.md)
[Sparse Voxel Storage and Management](#8435-sparse-voxel-storage-and-management.md) addresses the memory and performance bottlenecks of rendering high-resolution volumetric data by storing only occupied voxels in hierarchical structures (typically octrees) rather than dense grids. It solves the problem of excessive memory bandwidth and storage overhead inherent in naive voxel rendering. Unlike [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md), which processes every voxel in a fixed grid, this family leverages sparsity to skip empty space, enabling real-time rendering of complex scenes that would otherwise exceed VRAM limits.

## Background
The technique of rasterizing voxels as geometry has evolved alongside GPU capabilities [G]. Early implementations used OpenGL display lists for static volumes [G]. With the advent of vertex shaders and VBOs, explicit vertex buffers became standard [G]. More recent approaches leverage geometry shaders and instancing to handle larger datasets dynamically [G]. The method is widely used in scientific visualization, medical imaging, and real-time voxel-based [games](#12542-games-gaussian-mesh-splatting.md) [G].
